Multiple-response questions

Source: vignettes/articles/table-multiresponse.Rmd
table-multiresponse.Rmd
library(spicy)

table_multiresponse() tabulates one “check all that apply” question. Each item of the question is an indicator column, chosen or not, and one respondent can choose several items. The function reads the columns as one question: one row per item, with the number and the percentage of respondents who chose it. A last row gives the number of respondents behind the percentages.

With by, it compares groups. Each item gets a chi-squared test. The question gets a global test of all its items together, valid although one respondent can choose several items.

sochealth, the simulated survey shipped with spicy, has no such question, so this article builds one. Each respondent rated four domains of life from 1 to 5. A rating of 4 or 5 counts here as satisfied. The four logical columns then read like the answers to “Which of these domains of your life are you satisfied with? Check all that apply.”

domains <- data.frame(
  physical_activity = sochealth$physical_activity,
  health = sochealth$life_sat_health >= 4,
  work = sochealth$life_sat_work >= 4,
  relationships = sochealth$life_sat_relationships >= 4,
  standard = sochealth$life_sat_standard >= 4
)
head(domains, 4)
#>   physical_activity health  work relationships standard
#> 1                No   TRUE FALSE          TRUE     TRUE
#> 2                No   TRUE  TRUE          TRUE     TRUE
#> 3               Yes  FALSE FALSE          TRUE    FALSE
#> 4                No  FALSE  TRUE         FALSE    FALSE

A missing rating stays missing: 31 respondents have one or two, and none has all four. physical_activity, regular physical activity reported as Yes or No, serves as the grouping.

One question, several answers

A respondent can be satisfied with several domains, and most respondents are:

items <- c("health", "work", "relationships", "standard")
table(rowSums(domains[items], na.rm = TRUE))
#> 
#>   0   1   2   3   4 
#> 204 214 252 283 247

The 1200 respondents made 2555 choices: 204 of them chose no domain, and 782 chose two or more.

A tempting shortcut stacks the choices into one variable, one row per choice, and tabulates it like any categorical variable:

stacked <- data.frame(
  physical_activity = rep(domains$physical_activity, times = 4),
  domain = factor(rep(items, each = nrow(domains)), levels = items),
  chosen = unlist(domains[items], use.names = FALSE)
)
stacked <- stacked[stacked$chosen %in% TRUE, ]
nrow(stacked)
#> [1] 2555
table_categorical(stacked, select = domain, by = physical_activity)
#> Categorical table by physical_activity
#> 
#>  Variable        │ No n  No %  Yes n  Yes %  Total n  Total %   p    Cramer's V 
#> ─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  domain          │                                             .645     .03     
#>    health        │ 335   25.6   314   25.2     649     25.4                     
#>    work          │ 292   22.3   301   24.1     593     23.2                     
#>    relationships │ 375   28.7   336   26.9     711     27.8                     
#>    standard      │ 306   23.4   296   23.7     602     23.6

That table misreads the question in three ways.

  1. Its base is the choices. It has 2555 rows for 1200 respondents, and its percentages are shares of choices. They sum to 100 in each group, although one respondent can count in four rows.
  2. The respondents who chose nothing are gone. The 204 respondents without a domain left no row to stack.
  3. Its chi-squared test is not valid. The choices of one respondent are not independent observations. They violate “the assumption of independence among units required by all the usual tests of independence on contingency tables” (Loughin and Scherer, 1998, p. 631). The test also builds its expected counts on each group’s total of choices, where the question is about respondents (p. 632). In the simulations of Loughin and Scherer, it was “a horribly conservative procedure” (p. 636).

The third fault hides a real difference here. Active respondents choose more domains on average:

tapply(rowSums(domains[items], na.rm = TRUE), domains$physical_activity, mean)
#>       No      Yes 
#> 2.012308 2.267273

Every domain gains a little among them, so their shares of choices barely move: work is 24.1% of their choices, against 22.3%. Loughin and Scherer describe this case: “the units’ multiple responses mask real differences between the rows” (1998, p. 632). The share of respondents who chose work moves almost ten points, from 44.9% to 54.7%:

tbl <- table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = c(health, work, relationships, standard),
  by = physical_activity
)
tbl
#> Multiple responses by physical_activity
#> 
#>  Variable      │ No n  No %  Yes n  Yes %  Total n  Total %   p   
#> ───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  health        │ 335   51.5   314   57.1     649     54.1    .109 
#>  work          │ 292   44.9   301   54.7     593     49.4    .003 
#>  relationships │ 375   57.7   336   61.1     711     59.2    .233 
#>  standard      │ 306   47.1   296   53.8     602     50.2    .060 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents   │ 650          550           1200                  
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 204 respondents chose none of the items. Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test of each item by group. P-values adjusted via stats::p.adjust(method = "holm"); m = 4 test(s). Group comparison: Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-squared test of multiple marginal independence, χ²(3.16) = 17.36, p < .001.

Each percentage is now a share of the respondents of its group, and the Respondents row gives those bases. The note explains the percentages and names the tests. Its global test finds the difference the stacked table missed: p < .001, against .645. The rest of the article reads this table piece by piece.

A first table

Without by, the table describes the whole sample:

table_multiresponse(domains, select = c(health, work, relationships, standard))
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable        │   n       %    
#> ─────────────────┼────────────────
#>  health          │   649    54.1  
#>  work            │   593    49.4  
#>  relationships   │   711    59.2  
#>  standard        │   602    50.2  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │  1200          
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 204 respondents chose none of the items.

Four things to notice:

  1. One row per item. n counts the respondents who chose the item, and % is their share of the respondents of the base: the percentage of cases.
  2. The percentages sum to more than 100. Here they add up to 212.9, the mean number of choices per respondent times 100 (Jann, 2005, p. 107).
  3. The Respondents row is the base, the number of respondents every percentage is computed on.
  4. The note says what the percentages are of, which respondents form the base, and how many of them chose no item.

select takes tidyselect syntax, so select = health:standard gives the same table, as in the calls below.

Factor items and counted

Logical columns, like these, and numeric columns coded 0 and 1 are read as they are. A factor, character, or labelled column needs counted, the value that marks a choice. Three yes/no factors of sochealth show the case, and labels = TRUE prints their label attributes in place of their names:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
  counted = "Yes",
  labels = TRUE
)
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable                          │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────
#>  Current smoker                    │   249    20.8  
#>  Regular physical activity         │   550    45.8  
#>  Dentist visit in last 12 months   │   846    70.5  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents                       │  1200          
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 166 respondents chose none of the items.

counted applies to every selected column. Any other non-missing value counts as not chosen, and a missing value stays missing. A labelled column is chosen where its code or its value label equals counted. A value that matches nothing is an error, so a typo cannot produce a table of zeros:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
  counted = "yes"
)
#> Error in `table_multiresponse()`:
#> ! `counted = "yes"` matches no value of the selected columns.
#> ℹ Values found: "Yes", "No".

Labels and order

The rows show the column names by default. A named vector sets the wording you publish. sort = "desc" ranks the items by their total count, ties kept in questionnaire order:

table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  labels = c(
    health = "Health",
    work = "Work",
    relationships = "Relationships",
    standard = "Standard of living"
  ),
  sort = "desc"
)
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable             │   n       %    
#> ──────────────────────┼────────────────
#>  Relationships        │   711    59.2  
#>  Health               │   649    54.1  
#>  Standard of living   │   602    50.2  
#>  Work                 │   593    49.4  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents          │  1200          
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 204 respondents chose none of the items.

The default, sort = "questionnaire", keeps the order of select, normally the order of the questionnaire.

Bases and percentages

The base is the set of respondents a percentage of cases is computed on. Three bases are in use, and they differ on two kinds of respondents: those who chose nothing and those who skipped the question. Six invented respondents show the difference, for the question “How did you hear about the service? Check all that apply”:

heard <- data.frame(
  radio = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, NA, TRUE),
  press = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, NA, NA),
  web = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, NA, FALSE)
)
heard
#>   radio press   web
#> 1  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
#> 2  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
#> 3 FALSE  TRUE FALSE
#> 4 FALSE FALSE FALSE
#> 5    NA    NA    NA
#> 6  TRUE    NA FALSE

Respondent 4 chose nothing, respondent 5 skipped the question, and respondent 6 has one missing item.

The default, base = "valid", keeps every respondent with at least one non-missing item. Respondent 4 stays, and respondent 5 leaves:

table_multiresponse(heard, select = c(radio, press, web))
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable      │  n     %    
#> ───────────────┼─────────────
#>  radio         │  3    60.0  
#>  press         │  2    40.0  
#>  web           │  1    20.0  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents   │  5          
#> 
#> Respondents with no answer to the question removed: 1. Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 1 respondent chose none of the items.

Within the base, a missing item counts as not chosen, so respondent 6 counts for radio only. The note gives the number of respondents removed and the number who chose nothing. This is how expss counts its valid cases. It is also the base of Stata’s mrtab with its include option (Jann, 2005, p. 99). Jann uses that option in his own example, because its list of income types “is probably not exhaustive” (pp. 107-108).

base = "answered" keeps only the respondents who chose at least one item:

table_multiresponse(heard, select = c(radio, press, web), base = "answered")
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable      │  n     %    
#> ───────────────┼─────────────
#>  radio         │  3    75.0  
#>  press         │  2    50.0  
#>  web           │  1    25.0  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents   │  4          
#> 
#> Respondents with no answer to the question removed: 1. Respondents who chose no item removed: 1. Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who chose at least one item.

This is the default of SPSS MULT RESPONSE and of mrtab (Jann, 2005, p. 98). Under this base, choosing nothing cannot be told from skipping, so respondent 4 leaves with respondent 5, and the note counts two respondents removed. Jann states the dilemma: “it is often not clear a priori whether the respondent refused to answer the question (and thus should be excluded from analysis) or whether the correct response is simply ‘none’” (p. 107).

base = "all" keeps every row, as questionr::multi.table() does:

table_multiresponse(heard, select = c(radio, press, web), base = "all")
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable      │  n     %    
#> ───────────────┼─────────────
#>  radio         │  3    50.0  
#>  press         │  2    33.3  
#>  web           │  1    16.7  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents   │  6          
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: all respondents. 2 respondents chose none of the items.

Respondent 5 now counts as a respondent who chose nothing, and the note says that two did.

The counts are the same under the three bases. The percentages and the tests are not. "valid" assumes that a skipped question is coded missing on every item, and that a box left unchecked is coded FALSE or 0. In data that code an unchecked box as missing, "valid" would drop the respondents who checked nothing. "all" keeps them, along with those who skipped the question.

Percentages of cases or of responses

percent sets what a percentage is of. "cases", the default, divides by the respondents of the base. "responses" divides by all the choices made in the group, so the column sums to 100. "both" shows the two:

table_multiresponse(domains, select = health:standard, percent = "both")
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable        │   n      % of cases    % of responses  
#> ─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────
#>  health          │   649       54.1            25.4       
#>  work            │   593       49.4            23.2       
#>  relationships   │   711       59.2            27.8       
#>  standard        │   602       50.2            23.6       
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │  1200                                  
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages of respondents can sum to more than 100%; percentages of responses sum to 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 204 respondents chose none of the items.

The percentages of responses are the shares of the stacked table, and the note now describes both columns. The percentages of cases stay the default for three reasons. The papers on these tests tabulate them (Agresti and Liu, 1999, p. 937; Bilder and Loughin, 2004, p. 242). Jann finds that “usually, it is proportions on the basis of observations one is interested in” (2005, p. 98). And they are what the tests compare: for each item, the probability that a respondent of each group chooses it.

Comparing groups

tbl, the table of the first section, compares the active respondents with the others. With by, the counts and percentages are given for each group and for the Total margin. Rows with a missing by are removed, and the note says how many. The tests come in two layers: one per item, and one for the question.

One test per item

Each item gets the Pearson chi-squared test of its table of groups by chosen or not, on r − 1 degrees of freedom for r groups. The arithmetic is that of chisq.test(correct = FALSE): no continuity correction, and no constant added to an empty cell (Agresti and Liu, 1999). The data frame output keeps the statistics and both p-values:

wide <- table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  output = "data.frame"
)
wide[c("Variable", "Chi2", "df", "p", "p_unadjusted")]
#>        Variable      Chi2 df           p p_unadjusted
#> 1        health  3.698537  1 0.108920423 0.0544602116
#> 2          work 11.456128  1 0.002850345 0.0007125862
#> 3 relationships  1.425211  1 0.232547529 0.2325475286
#> 4      standard  5.415538  1 0.059874905 0.0199583016
#> 5   Respondents        NA NA          NA           NA

The p column is adjusted by Holm’s method, and p_unadjusted keeps the raw values. The items of one question form a natural family of tests, read together, so the adjustment is on by default. table_categorical() defaults to "none", because there each test belongs to a different variable.

The papers that test the items one by one adjust them by Bonferroni (Agresti and Liu, 1999, p. 941). Holm’s method controls the same family-wise error rate, whatever the dependence between the items. R’s documentation sees “no reason to use the unmodified Bonferroni correction because it is dominated by Holm’s method” (?p.adjust). Holm’s smallest adjusted p-value, .003 for work, equals the Bonferroni global p-value of Agresti and Liu (1999).

The note names the method and the number of items adjusted together. p_adjust = "none" keeps the raw p-values, and another method of stats::p.adjust() can be named instead. statistic = TRUE prints the statistics in a Test column, χ²(1) = 11.46 for work, with or without the p-values.

One test for the question

Agresti and Liu read the item tests as a follow-up: “When this overall test gives evidence against the null hypothesis, the separate chi-squared components provide information about the marginal tables that are responsible” (1999, p. 941). The overall test is the last sentence of the note. It tests multiple marginal independence: that the probability of choosing each item is the same in every group.

Its statistic is the sum of the item chi-squared statistics, 22.00 here. The sum does not depend on which answer of an item is coded as chosen (Agresti and Liu, 1999). It is not chi-squared under the null hypothesis: one respondent can choose several items, so the items are correlated (Loughin and Scherer, 1998). Its asymptotic distribution is a weighted sum of chi-squared variables, the weights being the eigenvalues of a design-effect matrix (Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton, 2000, Appendix A).

The mean of those weights is 1, but “individual weights may differ from one” (Thomas and Decady, 2004, p. 48). The default, test = "rs2", allows for their spread with the second-order Rao-Scott correction of Thomas and Decady (2004, pp. 48 and 58-59). It matches the first two moments of the distribution and refers the result to a chi-squared on fractional degrees of freedom: χ²(3.16) = 17.36 here. The result is deterministic.

glance() returns the global test as numbers:

broom::glance(tbl)[c("test_type", "statistic", "df", "p.value", "rs_cv")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   test_type statistic    df  p.value rs_cv
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 rs2            17.4  3.16 0.000707 0.516

rs_cv measures the spread of those weights: their coefficient of variation, their mean being taken as 1. It estimates the coefficient a of Thomas and Decady (2004, pp. 48 and 59). The correction divides the sum by 1 + rs_cv² and refers it to a chi-squared on c(r − 1)/(1 + rs_cv²) degrees of freedom, for c items and r groups (p. 48). Here 1 + 0.52² = 1.27, so 22.00 on 4 degrees of freedom becomes 17.36 on 3.16. The closer rs_cv is to 0, the less the correction changes. Thomas and Decady read this coefficient to decide whether the second order is needed (pp. 53 and 57).

The bootstrap

test = "bootstrap" refers the same sum to its distribution over boot_n resamples, 1999 by default. Each resample draws whole response vectors with replacement from the pooled respondents, with the group sizes held fixed (Loughin and Scherer, 1998). The p-value is the share of resamples whose sum is at least the observed one. It is random, so set a seed to reproduce it:

set.seed(1)
boot <- table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  test = "bootstrap"
)
broom::glance(boot)[c("test_type", "statistic", "df", "p.value", "boot_n")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   test_type statistic    df p.value boot_n
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 bootstrap      22.0    NA 0.00100   1999

The statistic is the uncorrected sum, 22.00, with no degrees of freedom. Two of the 1999 resamples reached it, so the p-value is 2/1999, printed as p = .001 in the note. A p-value of 0 would only say that no resample reached the sum. The note then reports it as below one resample in boot_n, rounded up.

A resample in which an item is chosen by every respondent or by none gives that item no statistic. It is drawn again, as Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton (2000, p. 1298) do, and attr(boot, "global_test")$boot_redraws counts the redraws. The bootstrap held its level in most published settings, with exceptions that Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton report (2000, p. 1305). No study of multiple marginal independence compares it with the second-order test.

Items nobody chose

An item chosen by every respondent, or by none, has no test, but its row stays. A fifth domain that nobody chose is added here on purpose:

with_empty <- transform(domains, spirituality = FALSE)
table_multiresponse(
  with_empty,
  select = health:spirituality,
  by = physical_activity
)
#> Multiple responses by physical_activity
#> 
#>  Variable      │ No n  No %  Yes n  Yes %  Total n  Total %    p   
#> ───────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  health        │ 335   51.5   314   57.1     649     54.1     .109 
#>  work          │ 292   44.9   301   54.7     593     49.4     .003 
#>  relationships │ 375   57.7   336   61.1     711     59.2     .233 
#>  standard      │ 306   47.1   296   53.8     602     50.2     .060 
#>  spirituality  │   0    0.0     0    0.0       0      0.0     –    
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents   │ 650          550           1200                   
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 204 respondents chose none of the items. Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test of each item by group. P-values adjusted via stats::p.adjust(method = "holm"); m = 4 test(s). Not tested (no variation, shown as –): spirituality. Group comparison: Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-squared test of multiple marginal independence, χ²(3.16) = 17.36, p < .001.

Its row shows a true zero and its p cell a dash, which the note explains. The item leaves the global test, which is unchanged, and the Holm adjustment, which still counts four tests. With fewer than two groups holding respondents, there is nothing to compare, and the table shows no test.

Descriptive tables

Some reports describe without testing. STROBE advises that “significance tests should be avoided in descriptive tables” (Vandenbroucke et al., 2007, p. 1643). A report on a small survey that reached nearly all of its population, for instance, may show no test at all.

p_value = FALSE removes the p column and the global test from every output, the data frames included. The first 80 respondents stand in for such a small survey:

small <- head(domains, 80)
table_multiresponse(
  small,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  p_value = FALSE,
  percent_digits = 0
)
#> Multiple responses by physical_activity
#> 
#>  Variable        │  No n    No %    Yes n    Yes %    Total n    Total %  
#> ─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  health          │   18      44      23       59        41         51     
#>  work            │   15      37      24       62        39         49     
#>  relationships   │   21      51      26       67        47         59     
#>  standard        │   19      46      21       54        40         50     
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │   41              39                 80                
#> 
#> Several answers possible: percentages are of respondents and can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents who answered the question, including those who chose no item. 12 respondents chose none of the items.

statistic stays independent of p_value, so statistic = TRUE would still show each item’s chi-squared. A p_adjust typed with p_value = FALSE is an error, since there is nothing to adjust.

percent_digits = 0 follows the AMA manual: “A percentage or decimal quotient should contain no more than the number of digits in the denominator” (American Medical Association, 2020, section 4.1.8). Groups of fewer than 100 respondents, 41 and 39 here, therefore take whole percentages.

The note answers two more rules. The AMA manual asks that “any discrepancy in the sum of percentages in a tabulation” be explained, and it names “multiple procedures” among the causes (section 18.7.2). JAMA’s instructions for tables ask authors to “explain any empty cells”. They also ask to “add a footnote to explain why numbers may not sum to group totals or percentages do not add to 100%” (JAMA Network, 2016, p. 2). The note says why the percentages of cases exceed 100, and what the dash of an untested item means. The Respondents row gives the denominator once for all the items, as the AMA manual allows for “a series of proportions or percentages drawn from the same sample” (section 18.7.3).

Citing a cell in running text

inline() returns one cell as the table prints it, so a number quoted in a sentence cannot drift from the table. An item is addressed by its column name. The groups are spanners, so model selects one, the Total margin included:

inline(tbl, work, column = "pct", model = "Yes")
#> [1] "54.7"
inline(tbl, work, column = "{n} ({pct}%)", model = "No")
#> [1] "292 (44.9%)"

The item p belongs to no group and is cited without model. The Respondents row is the fit statistic "nobs":

inline(tbl, work, column = "p")
#> [1] ".003"
inline(tbl, "nobs", model = "Yes")
#> [1] "550"

The statistic needs a table built with statistic = TRUE:

tbl_stat <- table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  statistic = TRUE
)
inline(tbl_stat, work, column = "statistic")
#> [1] "χ²(1) = 11.46"

Without column, inline() returns the count. In a grouped table it still needs model, and its error lists the groups. The global test has no cell: it lives in the note and in glance().

Downstream: the raw frame and the broom views

output = "data.frame" returns the wide frame at full precision: one row per item, a last row with the base, and columns named after the groups:

names(wide)
#>  [1] "Variable"     "No n"         "No %"         "Yes n"        "Yes %"       
#>  [6] "Total n"      "Total %"      "Chi2"         "df"           "p"           
#> [11] "p_unadjusted"

output = "long" returns one row per item and group, with the base of the group:

long <- table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  output = "long"
)
head(long, 3)
#>   variable group   n base      pct     chi2 df         p p_unadjusted
#> 1   health    No 335  650 51.53846 3.698537  1 0.1089204   0.05446021
#> 2   health   Yes 314  550 57.09091 3.698537  1 0.1089204   0.05446021
#> 3   health Total 649 1200 54.08333 3.698537  1 0.1089204   0.05446021

Both frames carry the note in attr(x, "note") and the global test in attr(x, "global_test").

tidy() returns one row per item and group, the margin flagged by total, with the proportions of respondents and of responses. glance() returns one row for the question:

broom::tidy(tbl)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 12
#>    variable      label   group total     n  base proportion proportion_responses
#>    <chr>         <chr>   <chr> <lgl> <int> <int>      <dbl>                <dbl>
#>  1 health        health  No    FALSE   335   650      0.515                0.256
#>  2 health        health  Yes   FALSE   314   550      0.571                0.252
#>  3 health        health  Total TRUE    649  1200      0.541                0.254

#>  5 work          work    Yes   FALSE   301   550      0.547                0.241

#>  8 relationships relati… Yes   FALSE   336   550      0.611                0.269
#>  9 relationships relati… Total TRUE    711  1200      0.592                0.278
#> 10 standard      standa… No    FALSE   306   650      0.471                0.234
#> 11 standard      standa… Yes   FALSE   296   550      0.538                0.237

#> # ℹ 4 more variables: statistic <dbl>, df <int>, p.value <dbl>,

broom::glance(tbl)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 11
#>   n_items n_items_tested n_groups  nobs test_type statistic    df p.value boot_n
#>     <int>          <int>    <int> <int> <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <int>
#> 1       4              4        2  1200 rs2            17.4  3.16 7.07e-4     NA
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: rs_cv <dbl>, p_adjust <chr>

Both column sets are fixed: a column the table does not show, such as boot_n under the Rao-Scott test, is present and NA. Index by name, never by position.

Comparison with other tools

Each tool settles the same four points in its own way: what a percentage is of, an item nobody chose, a respondent who did not answer, and the tests.

  • SPSS MULT RESPONSE computes percentages on cases by default (BASE = CASES), and its cross-tabulations show counts unless CELLS asks for percentages. An item nobody chose does not appear. Under the default MISSING = TABLE, a respondent who chose no item of a dichotomy group is missing, as under base = "answered". It offers no test.
  • Stata mrtab prints percentages of responses and of cases in its one-way table, and either one in a two-way table. It keeps the respondents with at least one response by default, include gives base = "valid", and includemissing gives base = "all" (Jann, 2005, pp. 98-99). Its overall Pearson test on the response patterns is “only suited if there are very few categories” (p. 115). mtest() tests each item, adjusted by bonferroni, holm or sidak, or not.
  • expss divides by the valid cases, those with at least one non-missing value (cross_cpct()), or by the responses (cross_cpct_responses()). Its column tests (significance_cpct()) are z tests, without Bonferroni adjustment by default.
  • questionr divides by every row in multi.table(), rows with all items missing included, and counts a missing item as not chosen. cross.multi.table() divides by the size of the group. An item nobody chose shows 0. It offers no test.
  • gtsummary, with type = "dichotomous", gives n (%) of the non-missing answers of each item, with an “Unknown” row for its missing values. A 0/1 item that nobody chose is an error unless it is a factor with a level 1. add_p() tests each item by a chi-squared test without continuity correction, or by Fisher’s exact test when an expected count is below 5. It adjusts nothing and has no global test.
  • MRCV gives counts, not percentages, and does not handle missing values. Its global tests are the bootstrap, the second-order Rao-Scott correction, and Bonferroni, all three by default. If an item lacks a 0 or a 1, every global test is NA. It adds 0.5 to the empty cells before each item statistic. table_multiresponse() reproduces its Rao-Scott test on the Kansas farmer data of Loughin and Scherer (1998), pinned in the package tests.

table_multiresponse() makes its four choices explicit: percentages of cases, the "valid" base with both counts in the note, items nobody chose kept at zero, and Holm-adjusted item tests with a Rao-Scott global test.

Output engines

The same table renders through six further engines, the console being the reference.

table_multiresponse(domains, select = health:standard, output = "gt")
table_multiresponse(domains, select = health:standard, output = "tinytable")
table_multiresponse(domains, select = health:standard, output = "flextable")
table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  output = "excel",
  excel_path = "domains.xlsx"
)
table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  output = "word",
  word_path = "domains.docx"
)
table_multiresponse(domains, select = health:standard, output = "clipboard")

A journal style moves the defaults of the whole table, as elsewhere in the family. Under style = "jama", p-values take two decimals, and three below .01:

table_multiresponse(
  domains,
  select = health:standard,
  by = physical_activity,
  style = "jama"
)
#> Multiple responses by physical_activity
#> 
#>  Variable      │ No n  No %  Yes n  Yes %  Total n  Total %   p
